content: Oklo is a region located near the town of Franceville in the Haut-Ogooué province of Gabon, a country in Central Africa. In September 1972, scientists discovered several natural nuclear fission reactors within the uranium mines in this area. This remarkable finding has sparked significant interest and curiosity among researchers. Gabon was a French colony when, in 1956, prospectors from the French nuclear energy agency (then the industrial division, later known as COGEMA) identified uranium deposits in this remote region. France quickly established mining operations near the village of Mounana, managed by the company Compagnie des Mines d'Uranium de Franceville (Comuf), to exploit these substantial mineral resources. The Gabonese government was granted a minority stake in the company. For four decades, France extracted uranium from Gabon, which was subsequently used to generate electricity in France and across much of Europe. Gabonese miners often joked that their efforts were the reason France's high-speed TGV trains could operate. However, the uranium deposits have since been depleted, and mining activities in the region have ceased. Currently, reclamation efforts are underway to address the environmental impact of the former mining operations. Geochemical evidence strongly suggests that the Oklo uranium deposit functioned as a natural nuclear fission reactor during Precambrian times. Some of the uranium extracted from the site was found to have a lower-than-expected concentration of the isotope uranium-235 (U-235), indicating that it had already undergone fission reactions. Geologists determined that this natural reactor was active approximately two billion years ago. At that time, the natural uranium contained about 3% U-235, a concentration sufficient to sustain a nuclear chain reaction when moderated by natural water.
